vignette: Eighteen months ago, during a supply run in a southern transit town, her life fractured. She delivered medical kits to a shelter when a patrol car pulled up. Officers were looking for a missing person. What followed was not a search, but a sweep. Maya watched from a doorway as they demanded identification from every unaccompanied adult in the courtyard. A man refused to lower his phone; a baton cracked his shoulder. Maya stepped forward to explain the triage bags on her cart. She remembers the heavy thud of a door locking, the precise weight of a knee pressing into her lower back, and the sudden smell of rubber and sweat. She remembers the cold tile against her cheek, the muffled voices, and the sharp yank of her cuffed wrists. She spent three hours on the ground before they realized their mistake. She walked away with bruised ribs and an unspoken vow never to stand between authority and its grip again. Afterward, her body never stopped waiting for the next command. At thirty-seven, she moves carefully, having learned that sudden movements draw attention. Her dark hair is pulled into a practical knot, the same style she wears when she navigates border camps or sorts through donation tents. In her aid office, she hears the squeak of rolling chairs and her breath catches. She scans the street outside her window, counting unmarked sedans. When a colleague walks by too quickly, she flinches, her pulse hammering until she forces it down. She stops sleeping. The dark is no longer rest; it is a space where the tile and the cuff marks press against her skin. She lies awake, replaying the officer's stance, the scrape of his boots, the exact second her voice lost its cadence. She tells her husband she is fine when he wakes her from a startle, her hand already reaching for the floor lamp. Her work demands openness. She negotiates logistics, comforts arriving families, and reads the subtle shifts in posture that signal trauma. But the line between her job and her survival has blurred. She avoids the uniformed security contractors who now patrol distribution centers. She cancels meetings when someone mentions "protocols." Last Tuesday, she watched a news report of a protest and immediately stood up, knocking over her water bottle. She cleaned the spill in silence, her hands shaking, while voices on the screen argued about control. She still visits the camps because she cannot abandon those who need listening. Yet she also admits she now counts the exits in every room, her mind quietly calculating the weight of a door, the speed of a siren, the distance to the nearest wall. I sit with her in the clinic, a coffee cup cooling between her palms. We have been meeting for six weeks, and I watch her trace the rim every time the hallway door clicks shut. She speaks of the camps in a steady voice, but her shoulders remain locked, her eyes fixed past my left shoulder. The world outside continues its ordinary rhythm, but inside Maya, time has not moved past that locked door. She breathes in, waits, and lets it out. I wait with her, watching her steady her own hands before she sets the cup down.
